name: SMAS imbrication flap

card.summary: A facelift technique that tightens the SMAS, the layer beneath facial skin, by overlapping or trimming it so the cheeks, jawline and neck are lifted and the lower face looks firmer.
card.note: Major surgery performed by a surgeon under anesthesia; risks include hematoma, nerve injury and scarring.

quick.overview:
The SMAS (superficial musculoaponeurotic system) is a fibrous layer under the facial skin that connects to the facial muscles. In SMAS imbrication, the surgeon overlaps and sutures this layer, or removes a strip of it in a SMASectomy, so that sagging cheek and jowl tissue is repositioned upward. The visible payoff is a tighter jawline, smoother jowls and a firmer neck contour rather than a skin pull alone.

The approach grew out of the SMAS concept described in 1976 and is one of several facelift options, alongside plication, SMAS flaps and deep plane lifts. Reviews describe lateral SMASectomy as a widely used, reproducible technique, and meta-analyses compare complication rates across SMAS methods.
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic or facial plastic surgeon, usually through incisions around the ear and into the hairline, often combined with skin redraping, neck work or fat grafting. Recovery in the facelift literature is typically a few weeks of swelling and bruising, with results judged over months.
quick.risks: Reported complications of SMAS facelifts include hematoma, temporary or permanent nerve injury, scarring, hair loss near incisions and skin necrosis, which is more frequent in smokers. A 2019 meta-analysis found complication rates differed modestly between SMAS techniques.

lead: SMAS imbrication is a facelift technique in which the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), a layer of connective tissue and muscle fascia lying between facial skin and deeper structures, is tightened by overlapping its edges. A closely related variant, lateral SMASectomy, removes a strip of SMAS and sutures the edges together [1][2]. In both, the surgeon lifts the deeper support layer instead of relying on skin tension alone.

For appearance, the purpose is rejuvenation and definition of the lower two thirds of the face and neck: lifting jowls, restoring the jawline and softening cheek and neck laxity [2][3]. Surgeons who favour SMASectomy describe it as producing a lift similar to a traditional SMAS flap without as much nerve-injury risk [1].

Facelift literature includes reviews of technique, a 2019 meta-analysis of 183 studies comparing complications between SMAS methods, and surgeon-reported series on short-scar facelifts using lateral SMASectomy [1][4][5].

angle.text: By tightening the SMAS rather than only the skin, the technique lifts sagging jowls and cheeks, producing a more defined jawline and lower-face contour.

paras: The SMAS was described in 1976 by Mitz and Peyronie, and SMAS-based facelifting became the standard approach after the technique of Tord Skoog [6]. Wikipedia distinguishes plication, in which the SMAS is folded and sutured with limited dissection, from flap or imbrication techniques in which the layer is elevated and repositioned [6]. In lateral SMASectomy, a portion of SMAS over the junction of mobile and fixed tissue is resected, and a review describes this as giving a strong lift while allowing the vector of pull to be adjusted to the patient's face [1].

A 2007 review of major rhytidectomy techniques lists traditional rhytidectomy, deep-plane and composite lifts, limited-incision approaches such as lateral SMASectomy, S-lift and MACS-lift, and suspension suture lifts [2].

Short-scar versions pair SMASectomy with limited incisions, and a 2003 review reports high patient satisfaction and low morbidity for lateral SMASectomy while noting that younger patients often need less extensive procedures [3]. Facelifts are often combined with fat grafting, which a 2021 systematic review examined for safety and effectiveness compared with facelift alone [7]. A prospective 1996 study compared lateral and standard SMAS facelifts with extended SMAS and composite techniques [8].

A 2019 meta-analysis in Aesthetic Surgery Journal pooled 183 studies and categorized techniques as SMAS plication, SMASectomy/imbrication, SMAS flap, high lateral SMAS flap, deep plane and composite. Temporary nerve injury was highest with high lateral SMAS (1.85 percent) and composite rhytidectomy (1.52 percent) compared with plication, while permanent nerve injury did not differ among techniques [4].

A 2019 Clinics in Plastic Surgery review of lateral SMASectomy describes it as safe, versatile and reproducible [1]. A 678-case comparison examined tumescent infiltration to reduce complications in facelifts [9]. A 2022 paper quantified skin removal across facelift approaches [10].

Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common facelift complication, followed by sensory and motor nerve injury, skin necrosis (about twelve-fold higher in smokers), scarring, hair loss at incisions and ear displacement [6]. Recovery for facelifts is reported as two to four weeks depending on technique, and longevity varies by technique and patient [6].
